text:
This line chart shows how validation loss changes during training for three methods.

The horizontal axis is training step, labeled from zero to ten thousand in increments of two thousand. The vertical axis is cross-entropy loss, with no units specified. Its labels run from one point five to four point five in increments of zero point five. Both axes are linear, and the loss axis does not start at zero.

The legend identifies Baseline in blue, plus LoRA in orange, and Full fine-tune in green.

All three start at their highest loss, about four point five, and reach about two point seven five by step two thousand. At step four thousand, loss is about two point two six for Baseline, two point one three for plus LoRA, and two point zero six for Full fine-tune. At step ten thousand, the values are about two point zero eight, one point eight six, and one point six three, respectively. The lowest visible value is about one point six two for Full fine-tune near step nine thousand two hundred fifty.

All three losses fall steeply at first, then decline more slowly. The lines are close together early on but separate later. Baseline levels off first and finishes highest, plus LoRA finishes in the middle, and Full fine-tune finishes lowest.

This vertical bar chart compares ImageNet top-one accuracy across five models.

The horizontal axis is labeled Model. The vertical axis is labeled Top-one accuracy, in percent. Its scale is linear and starts at 70 rather than zero, with ticks every two percentage points up to 88.

From left to right, the five blue bars represent ResNet-50, ViT-B slash 16, ConvNeXt-T, Swin-T, and Ours.

ResNet-50 scores 76.1 percent. ViT-B slash 16 scores 81.8 percent. ConvNeXt-T scores 82.1 percent. Swin-T scores 81.3 percent. Ours scores 84.6 percent.

Ours ranks highest, 2.5 percentage points above ConvNeXt-T, the runner-up. The three middle bars cluster within 0.8 percentage points of each other. ResNet-50 ranks lowest, 8.5 percentage points below Ours.

This grouped bar chart compares scores across three benchmarks for three model sizes.

The horizontal axis is labeled Benchmark. The vertical axis is labeled Score, with no units specified. Its scale is linear and starts at 50 rather than zero, with ticks every 10 up to 100.

From left to right, the benchmark groups are GLUE, SuperGLUE, and SQuAD F1. The legend is labeled Model size. Within each group, the bars run from Small in blue to Base in orange to Large in green.

In that size order, the GLUE scores are about 78, 84, and 89. The SuperGLUE scores are about 65, 71, and 79. The SQuAD F1 scores are about 83, 88, and 91.

Scores rise with model size on every benchmark. The increase from Small to Large is greatest for SuperGLUE, at about 14 points. At every size, SQuAD F1 scores highest, GLUE is next, and SuperGLUE scores lowest.

This four-by-four confusion matrix is a heat map showing how test set predictions compare with true labels.

The horizontal axis shows the predicted label, and the vertical axis shows the true label. Both axes are categorical. The color key runs from pale blue for lower counts to dark blue for higher counts, with labeled ticks from zero to eighty in steps of twenty.

The categories are cat, dog, bird, and car, in that order both from left to right and from top to bottom.

Reading across each row in predicted-label order: for true cat, the counts are eighty-eight, nine, two, and one. For true dog, they are eleven, eighty-four, three, and two. For true bird, they are three, four, ninety, and three. For true car, they are zero, one, two, and ninety-seven.

The dark diagonal stands out: correct predictions dominate every row. Car has the most correct predictions, followed by bird, cat, and dog. The two largest errors are between cats and dogs: eleven dogs were labeled cat, and nine cats were labeled dog. No cars were labeled cat.

This heatmap, titled “Layer 6, head 3 attention,” shows attention values for pairs of tokens in the sentence “The cat sat on the mat.”

The horizontal axis is labeled “Key token,” and the vertical axis is labeled “Query token.” Both axes are categorical. The categories, from left to right and from top to bottom, are capital T The, cat, sat, on, lowercase the, mat, and a period. The linear color scale on the right runs from zero in dark purple to one in yellow, with ticks every zero point two.

Along the diagonal, where the query and key are the same token, attention is about one for capital T The, about zero point nine one for cat, about zero point eight two for sat, about zero point eight four for on, about zero point seven four for lowercase the, about zero point three eight for mat, and about zero point six two for the period.

The diagonal has the highest value in every row except mat. In that row, attention to cat is about zero point four seven, higher than attention to mat itself. All cells above the diagonal are at or near zero, and most cells below it are also dark purple.

This scatter plot shows how M M L U scores vary with parameter count across three model families.

The horizontal axis is parameter count in billions. It runs from about 3 to 72, with labels every 10 billion from 10 to 70. The vertical axis is M M L U in percent. It runs from just under 55 to about 88, with labels every 5 percentage points from 55 to 85. Both axes are linear, and neither starts at zero.

The legend, titled Family, identifies Dense as blue circles, M o E as orange crosses, and Distilled as green squares.

Dense starts at about 57 percent at 6 billion parameters, peaks at about 87 percent at 65 billion, and ends at about 85 percent at 68 billion. M o E starts at about 56 percent at 6 billion, reaches about 75 percent at 22 billion, and ends at its peak of about 87 percent at 66 billion. Distilled starts at about 61 percent at 11 billion, peaks at about 82 percent at 68 billion, and ends at about 78 percent just beyond 68 billion.

Scores generally rise with parameter count, though not steadily. At comparable counts in the middle of the plot, M o E generally scores highest and Distilled lowest. Near 66 billion, the highest Dense and M o E scores nearly coincide.

This box and whisker plot compares the distribution of inference latency across four types of hardware.

The horizontal axis is labeled Hardware and is categorical. The vertical axis is labeled Latency in milliseconds. Its scale is linear, with ticks from zero to 175 in steps of 25. The plotting area extends slightly below zero and up to about 200 milliseconds.

From left to right, the groups are CPU, GPU, TPU, and Edge NPU.

For the CPU, the median is about 116 milliseconds. The box spans about 106 to 141 milliseconds, and the whiskers reach about 68 and 190. For the GPU, the median is about 16 milliseconds, the box spans about 14 to 20, and the whiskers reach about 10 and 28. For the TPU, the median is about 12 milliseconds, the box spans about 9 to 14, and the whiskers reach about 7 and 20. For the Edge NPU, the median is about 45 milliseconds, the box spans about 38 to 48, and the whiskers reach about 24 and 62.

The CPU has the highest median and the widest spread, followed in median latency by the Edge NPU, GPU, and TPU. High outliers appear at about 29 milliseconds for the GPU, around 22 to 24 for the TPU, and from about 65 to 87 for the Edge NPU. No CPU outliers are marked.

This split violin chart compares score distributions with and without chain-of-thought prompting across three tasks.

The horizontal axis, labeled Task, lists Math, Code, and Writing from left to right. The vertical axis, labeled Score, is linear and does not start at zero. It extends from about 18 to 110, with labeled ticks from 20 to 100 in steps of 20. No score unit is shown.

The legend is labeled Condition. For each task, the blue left half is Without CoT, and the orange right half is With CoT. Wider portions indicate a greater concentration of scores.

The three horizontal marks in each half show the lower quartile, median, and upper quartile. For Math, these are about 48, 56, and 62 without prompting, versus about 67, 74, and 79 with prompting. For Code, they are about 49, 55, and 62 without, versus about 58, 64, and 70 with. For Writing, they are about 48, 54, and 61 without, versus about 48, 56, and 64 with.

Without prompting, the three tasks have similar medians. With prompting, Math shows the largest median increase, about 18 points, followed by Code at about 9 points. Writing changes least, with a median increase of about 2 points and substantial overlap between conditions.

Two overlaid histograms with smooth curves show how logit margins are distributed across two groups.

The horizontal axis is labeled logit margin, with ticks from minus three to five and no unit shown. The vertical axis is labeled count, starting at zero with ticks every twenty-five up to one hundred seventy-five. Both axes are linear.

The legend, titled Split, identifies blue as in-distribution and orange as out-of-distribution.

The tallest blue bar reaches about one hundred seventy-five at a margin of about minus zero point three. The blue curve peaks there at about one hundred sixty. The tallest orange bar reaches about one hundred fifty at a margin of about three point one, where the orange curve peaks at about one hundred thirty-five. Both curves approach zero in their tails: the blue near minus three point one and three point five, and the orange near one and four point seven.

Each group has one main peak. The blue distribution is broader, with a higher peak and generally lower margins. The orange distribution is more tightly clustered around three. The curves cross at a margin of about one point nine, at a count of about twenty-five.

This scatter plot shows throughput rising with compute, with a reported correlation of zero point nine four.

The horizontal axis is GPU hours in thousands, labeled from zero to ten in steps of two. It extends slightly beyond those labels at both ends. The vertical axis is tokens per second in thousands, labeled from five to twenty-five in steps of five. It spans about one to twenty-seven thousand and does not start at zero. Both axes are linear.

There is one unlabeled series of blue dots, with a straight blue fitted line and a pale blue band around it. There is no legend.

The fitted line rises from about five thousand tokens per second near zero GPU hours to about twenty-five thousand tokens per second at nine thousand nine hundred GPU hours. The lowest dot is at about two thousand five hundred tokens per second and six hundred fifty GPU hours. The highest is at about twenty-six thousand tokens per second and eight thousand six hundred GPU hours.

The dots cluster around the rising line across the range. Notable departures include a dot above the line at about seven hundred fifty GPU hours and twelve thousand tokens per second, and one below it at about six thousand three hundred GPU hours and twelve thousand seven hundred tokens per second.

This line chart, titled “Scaling of test error with data,” shows test error decreasing as dataset size increases for three optimizers.

The horizontal axis, labeled “Dataset size” in tokens, is logarithmic, with labeled ticks from one million to ten billion, each ten times the previous one. The vertical axis, labeled “Error,” has no stated units. It is linear and does not start at zero. It spans about 0.75 to 3.15, with labeled ticks from 1 to 3 in steps of 0.5.

The legend, titled “Optimizer,” identifies S G D in blue, Adam in orange, and Muon in green. Each line has circular markers and a narrow shaded band.

In that order, all three errors start at about 2.98 at one million tokens, their highest values. At ten million tokens, the errors are about 2.42, 2.31, and 2.27. At one hundred million, they are about 1.99, 1.88, and 1.70. At one billion, they are about 1.63, 1.45, and 1.27. At ten billion, they reach their lowest values: about 1.34, 1.15, and 0.91.

Every line falls at every step. After the nearly shared starting point, S G D consistently has the highest error, Adam is in the middle, and Muon has the lowest. The gap between S G D and Muon grows to about 0.43 by the end.

This two-panel line chart shows how training and validation accuracy change with epoch, and how final validation accuracy varies with learning rate.

In the left panel, A, titled Accuracy, the horizontal axis is Epoch, labeled from zero to 30 in steps of five. The vertical axis is Accuracy, with labels from 0.3 to 1 in steps of 0.1. Both axes are linear, and the vertical axis does not start at zero. In the right panel, B, titled Learning-rate sweep, the horizontal axis is Learning rate, on a logarithmic scale labeled 0.0001, 0.001, and 0.01. The vertical axis is Final validation accuracy, with a linear scale starting just above 0.6 and labeled from 0.65 to 0.90.

Panel A labels the blue line Train and the orange line Validation. Panel B has one blue line with square markers.

Both curves start at about 0.26 at epoch one and reach about 0.92 at epoch 12, marked by a dashed vertical line. Training accuracy approaches 1 by epoch 30. Validation accuracy peaks at about 0.945 near epoch 17 and ends at about 0.87. In panel B, at learning rates of 0.0001, 0.0003, 0.001, 0.003, and 0.01, the accuracies are about 0.81, 0.86, 0.89, 0.84, and 0.62, respectively.

The epoch curves initially overlap, then diverge as training accuracy levels off and validation accuracy declines. The sweep peaks at the middle rate and drops most sharply at the highest rate.

This three-panel line chart shows how accuracy changes over training epochs for two augmentation settings on each dataset.

All three panels use the same linear scales. The horizontal axis, labeled Epoch, has ticks from zero to 100 in steps of 25. The vertical axis, labeled Accuracy, shows accuracy as a fraction, with ticks from zero to 0.8 in steps of 0.2. The plotting area extends slightly below zero and up to about 1.

From left to right, the panels are CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet. The legend is titled Augmentation. Blue means None, and orange means RandAugment.

All six curves start at about zero. On CIFAR-10, accuracy at epoch 50 is about 0.83 without augmentation and 0.88 with RandAugment. At epoch 100, the values are about 0.91 and 0.94, respectively. RandAugment peaks at about 0.95 near epoch 90. On CIFAR-100, the values in the same order are about 0.64 and 0.69 at epoch 50, ending at about 0.69 and 0.75. On Tiny-ImageNet, they are about 0.50 and 0.55 at epoch 50, ending at about 0.55 and 0.60.

Accuracy rises fastest early and then levels off. RandAugment stays above no augmentation after the start. For both settings, CIFAR-10 finishes highest, followed by CIFAR-100, then Tiny-ImageNet.

This single-panel dot-and-error-bar chart shows mean BLEU scores for four model variants in an ablation study, with error bars extending one standard deviation above and below each mean over five seeds.

The horizontal axis, labeled Variant, is categorical. The vertical axis, labeled BLEU, is linear and does not start at zero. It spans about 55.3 to 73.6 BLEU points, with labeled ticks from 57.5 to 72.5 in steps of 2.5.

From left to right, the categories are Full model, minus attention, minus residual, and minus norm. Each blue dot marks a mean.

The full model averages about 71.5, with an error bar from about 70.3 to 72.8. Minus attention averages about 65.3, spanning about 64.2 to 66.4. Minus residual averages about 56.5, spanning about 56.2 to 56.9. Minus norm averages about 66.6, spanning about 65.0 to 68.2.

The full model scores highest. Minus norm ranks second, slightly above minus attention, and their error bars overlap. Minus residual is lowest by a wide margin, about 15 BLEU points below the full model, and has the shortest error bar.

This nine-panel scatterplot matrix, titled Feature pairs by species, shows how three flower measurements vary together across three species groups.

The axes are linear, with no units shown. From left to right, the horizontal axes are petal length, spanning about 0.3 to 6.6, petal width, about minus 0.3 to 2.6, and sepal length, about 3.6 to 7.9. From top to bottom, the vertical axes follow the same order and ranges in the scatterplots. Only the petal width range includes zero. In the top row, petal length is shown first as distribution curves, then against petal width and sepal length. The middle row shows petal width against petal length, then width distributions, then petal width against sepal length. The bottom row shows sepal length against petal length and petal width, then sepal length distributions. Curve heights have no separately labeled scale.

The species legend identifies blue as setosa-like, orange as versicolor-like, and green as virginica-like.

In that species order, petal length distributions peak at about 1.6, 4.3, and 5.5. Petal width peaks are about 0.3, 1.4, and 2.0. Sepal length peaks are about 5.1, 5.8, and 6.5.

The groups cluster from blue at the lowest values to green at the highest for all three measurements. Petal length and width together separate the clusters clearly. Sepal lengths overlap more, particularly between orange and green; the highest orange point reaches about 7.1.

This clustered heat map shows normalized task scores for five rows across six tasks, with branching trees showing how the rows and columns group together.

There is one panel. The horizontal axis lists tasks, and the vertical axis lists M labels. Both axes are categorical. The color key marks zero point five near white and one at dark red. Darker blue indicates lower scores; the blue endpoint is unlabeled.

From left to right, the columns are Trans, Code, Math, Summ, Q A, and N L I. From top to bottom, the rows are M three, M four, M two, M one, and M five.

In column order, approximate scores read from color are as follows. M three: about point seven, one, point eight, point four, near zero, and near zero. M four: about point six, point eight, point eight, point five, point three, and point one. M two: about point one, point two, point two, point five, point eight, and point four. M one: about point three, point one, point one, point eight, point six, and point seven. M five: about point two, near zero, point one, point eight, point seven, and point eight.

The trees group the first three tasks separately from the last three. M three and M four cluster together and score higher on the first three tasks. M one and M five pair closely and show the reverse pattern. M two joins that pair but peaks on Q A.

This cumulative line chart, titled “Response length distribution,” compares the proportions of responses at or below a given length for two decoding methods.

The horizontal axis, labeled “Tokens generated,” has ticks from zero to 1,600 in steps of 200, with a small margin beyond each end. The vertical axis, labeled “Proportion,” runs from zero to one in steps of zero point two. Both scales are linear.

The legend, titled “Decoding,” identifies Greedy in blue and Speculative in orange.

Both curves start near zero tokens at a proportion of zero. The halfway point is about 100 tokens for Speculative and about 260 for Greedy. At 200 tokens, about 86 percent of Speculative responses and about 40 percent of Greedy responses are at or below that length. At 400 tokens, the proportions are about 99 percent and 73 percent, respectively. The orange curve reaches one at about 450 tokens. The blue curve reaches about 99 percent by 1,000 tokens and extends along the top of the chart to about 1,580 tokens.

The orange curve rises more steeply and levels off earlier. Speculative responses are generally shorter, while Greedy has a longer tail.

This horizontal bar chart shows the number of surveyed papers at each of six venues. The horizontal axis, labeled count, is linear and starts at zero, with labeled ticks every 50 papers through 400. The scale extends to about 430. The vertical axis, labeled Venue, lists NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL, CVPR, and EMNLP from top to bottom. Each venue has one muted red bar, with no separate legend.

NeurIPS has about 411 papers, ICML about 304, ICLR about 376, ACL about 157, CVPR about 288, and EMNLP about 132. NeurIPS has the most papers, followed by ICLR. ICML and CVPR are close to each other, on either side of 300. ACL and EMNLP have substantially fewer papers than the other four, with EMNLP lowest.
